transcript.speech: What makes a good error message?
This is part 5 of my series of building with good UX.
In the last few parts we went deep on loading states, and now we're going to error states.
And if you're building with AI tools, unless you specifically ask for it, most tools are pretty bad at creating error states by default.
First is your error message should never be your database or backend logic just dumped on the screen.
One being, how would a regular person even know what that means?
And two, this could also be a security vulnerability if you're exposing details about your app's backend.
Okay, so then you just put 'something went wrong', right? Wrong.
Your user doesn't need to know the technical details, but they do need something less vague than that.
Think about it. If you enter your card information and you press pay, and it says 'something went wrong',
you have no idea if your payment went through or not. That is a pretty terrible user experience.
A good error message does three things: it tells them what happened, why it happened, and gives them a clear action.
So instead of saying 'something went wrong', you say: 'Your payment didn't go through. Your card was declined. Please check your card details or try a different payment method.'
Now the user knows exactly what happened, why, and what's next.
And then there's the worst kind of error: the silent failure. No message at all.
The user clicks submit, the button does nothing, the screen doesn't change. They don't know if it worked, if it broke.
And this is what a lot of vibe coding AI tools generate by default. So you need to know these things to know what to ask for.
In the next video, we're going to talk about forms and how a lot of people don't feel like filling them out,
and how to design them so that your user hates you a little less. So follow for more.

visual_demonstrations.observation: A mobile UI demonstrates a photo upload failure showing a raw technical error popup modal containing internal backend error codes ('userID: 34fd3d4dfjnke out of storage capacity', 'STORAGE_QUOTA_EXCEEDED', trace IDs).
visual_demonstrations.before: A mobile screen showing a photo being uploaded with an 'Uploading...' spinner button.
visual_demonstrations.after: A red modal overlays with technical backend error trace information.

visual_demonstrations.observation: A payment form with credit card fields is submitted by clicking 'Pay $99.00', which shows a vague top banner saying 'Something went wrong'.
visual_demonstrations.before: Card details filled out in form fields above 'Pay $99.00' button.
visual_demonstrations.after: A red banner with an exclamation mark appears above the title stating 'Something went wrong'.

visual_demonstrations.observation: The payment form submission displays an improved informative banner stating: 'Your payment didn't go through / Your card was declined. Please check your card details or try a different payment method.'
visual_demonstrations.before: Payment form filled out before clicking 'Pay $99.00'.
visual_demonstrations.after: The descriptive error alert banner appears with explanation and recovery instructions.

visual_demonstrations.observation: A 'Submit' button is repeatedly clicked with a mouse cursor, but the button state and screen do not respond or give feedback, leaving the user unsure if the action succeeded.
visual_demonstrations.before: A black 'Submit' button centered on a white screen.
visual_demonstrations.after: Cursor clicks repeatedly on 'Submit'; text 'Did that even work?' appears above the button without any confirmation or error state.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Do not dump raw database errors or backend logic directly onto the user's screen, because regular users will not understand it and exposing backend implementation details is a security risk.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: Demonstration of raw database exception code and a technical backend trace popup on a mobile screen.
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Raw backend error traces confuse non-technical users and expose internal system architecture/security vulnerabilities.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Handle errors cleanly without showing raw backend/database error logs in the client UI.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Hide database stack traces, internal IDs, and raw server logs from the user interface.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Standard users cannot interpret technical stack traces, and leaking server details creates security vulnerabilities.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Any application encountering server, database, or API errors.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Avoid vague messages like 'something went wrong'. A good error message must fulfill three criteria: explain what happened, explain why it happened, and provide a clear action for the user to resolve it.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: Side-by-side comparison of a checkout form showing 'Something went wrong' versus 'Your payment didn't go through. Your card was declined. Please check your card details or try a different payment method.'
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Vague error messages leave users confused about whether their transaction or action succeeded and what they should do next.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Write descriptive error messages that specify the failure, the underlying reason, and next steps.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Replace generic alert banners with specific text explaining the issue and recovery options.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Users need to know the state of their action (e.g., whether money was charged) and how to fix the issue.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Forms, payments, and interactive submission flows.

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Never allow silent failures where an action button does nothing and provides no visual feedback.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: A 'Submit' button clicked repeatedly with no state change, leaving the screen static.
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Users do not know whether the system received their input, crashed, or succeeded.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Always provide clear visual feedback or an error message when an action fails.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Ensure button interactions trigger appropriate visual states or explicit error notifications.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: Silent failure is the worst user experience because the user is left completely uninformed.

analyst_interpretation.interpretation: The video highlights three common error-handling anti-patterns (raw technical error dumps, vague generic errors, and silent failure states) and prescribes actionable, user-centric error messaging with clear status, rationale, and resolution guidance.
inferences_not_shown_or_said: Specific accessibility requirements such as ARIA live regions or screen-reader announcements are not discussed in the video.

spot_check_visuals.observation: A graphic displays three loading state UI types labeled 'Skeleton screen', 'Spinner', and 'Progress bar'.
A payment modal shows a red callout banner reading 'Your payment didn't go through' with body text 'Your card was declined. Please check your card details or try a different payment method.'
